description: Low-country county (c. 900–1428) that reclaimed polders from the North Sea to become a prosperous trading region; its later incorporation into the Burgundian Netherlands positioned it as the future core of Dutch commercial dominance, while its herring fishery and North Sea trade established maritime patterns that would define the later Dutch Republic.

temporal.notes: Dominant Low Countries polity; Burgundian absorption.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Dirk I and Dirk II establish comital power over the Rhine delta.
Polder reclamation and trade growth; Holland expands into Zeeland and Frisia.
Floris V consolidates; Holland is the dominant county of the Low Countries.
Hooks and Cods civil war; Burgundian acquisition ends independence.

rise_factors.description: The Rhine-Meuse delta gave access to major European trade arteries; Holland became the nexus of North Sea commerce.
Peat extraction, herring fisheries, and reclaimed polders generated sustained revenue independent of agricultural cycles.
Counts granted early town charters to Dordrecht, Haarlem, and Delft, fostering urban commercial networks.

Holland's access to the North Sea herring grounds, and the development of the curing technique that preserved herring for long-distance trade (c.14th c.), made Dutch herring a major European commodity. The herring fishery funded Holland's early commercial expansion.

Holland's position at the Rhine delta gave it control of the main artery of German trade to the North Sea. The toll at Dordrecht became a major revenue source, and Holland merchants inserted themselves as intermediaries in the Baltic-Rhine commercial axis.

Systematic peat reclamation (10th–12th centuries) converted coastal bogs into agricultural land, dramatically increasing Holland's productive area. The associated drainage technology expertise later became the basis for Dutch hydraulic engineering dominance.

decline_factors.description: The Hooks and Cods civil war (1350–1490) created endemic factional violence that exhausted comital resources.
Philip the Good of Burgundy absorbed Holland through purchase and negotiated inheritance 1428–1432.
Noble and urban factions prevented a unified response to Burgundian pressure.

Habsburg acquisition of Holland (1433–77) through the Burgundian inheritance route incorporated the county into the Low Countries complex under Charles V. Holland lost direct political autonomy but gained access to the vast Habsburg commercial network.
